To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of ambarbital on schedule performance are rate-dependent and that these effects are influenced by the discriminative stimuli present during odd-numbered intervals.

the effects of drugs on behavior are not simply a function of the drug's effect on the rate of responding, but that the effects of the drug on responding are a function of the interaction between the drug and the discriminative stimulus conditions.

amobarbital increases responding under a 10-minute fixed-interval schedule, that the effects are inversely related to baseline rates of responding, and that the effects of amabarbital on responding during odd-numberd minutes are dependent upon stimulus change.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of drugs on schedule-controlled behavior in a multiple schedule of reinforcement.
the rate-dependent effects of drugs on schedule-controlled behavior and the modification of these effects by discriminative stimuli.

the effects of drugs on behavior maintained under a schedule of reinforcement in which the stimulus change during reinforcement is either the same as that during nonreinforcement (Experiment 1), or different from that during nonreforcement (Experiment 2).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of ambarbital on responding during even- and odd-minute intervals were similar in the sense that they were both inversely related to baseline rates.

the effects of ambarbital on responding during odd-number-old minutes were less than predicted on basis of control rates of responding, but the degree to which this was so depended on the nature of the stimulus change and the control rates.
the rate-increasing effects of a drug are dependent on the control rate of responding, and on the stimulus conditions under which responding is measured.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the rate of responding is an important variable determining the effects of drugs on schedule-controlled behavior; that this relationship is modified by discriminative stimuli; and that the modification is a function of the nature of the discriminative stimuli.
the effects of ambarbital on responding are inversely related to the control rates of responding, but that these effects may also be modified by the nature of the stimulus change.

amobarbital has rate-dependent effects, that these are modulated by the discriminative stimulus conditions, and that the stimulus conditions that modulate the effects of amabarbitol on rate also modulate the effects on control rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of drugs on behavior are not simply a function of the drug's effects on response rates.
the effects of drugs on behavior depend on the context in which the behavior occurs.
